RESEARCH NOTES / VERSION 1.0

Built on curiosity.
Grounded in evidence.

01

A deliberately simplified world

A 32-panel habitat contains hidden loose fasteners, delamination or microcracks. Each defect changes four normalised sensor features. Seeded Gaussian noise creates imperfect measurements.

This is a conceptual simulator, not a finite-element solver, a digital twin calibrated to a spacecraft, or a flight-certified diagnostic system.

02

Model-based artificial intelligence

A Bayesian classifier evaluates healthy material and three defect types over five severity levels. It updates posterior beliefs after each reading. It has no access to the hidden defect array.

The active policy balances unmeasured panels, uncertain diagnoses and neighbours of anomalies. This is an explicit heuristic, not an optimal information-gain claim or a pretrained neural network.

03

Robotics with constraints

Two agents move between inspection panels. Travel costs time and energy; the scheduler selects the nearest available robot. Disable either agent and the remaining agent takes over.

Motion is a panel-level abstraction. Collision avoidance, manipulator dynamics and microgravity contact forces are outside this model.

04

Repair is a hypothesis, too

Interventions are matched to defect types and can fail. After each repair, old evidence is cleared and three fresh measurements test for residual anomalies. Isolation stops simulated growth but does not remove damage.

Forecasts use the same assumed growth law. Real-world transfer requires experimental vibration data, calibration and independent validation.

Try a three-minute mission

  1. Open Judge mode. Place two hidden defects and seal the scenario.
  2. Start inspection. Disable one robot and watch the mission adapt.
  3. Open Diagnostics to inspect the measurements and competing hypotheses.
  4. Use Repair lab, then review the fresh verification readings.
  5. Reveal ground truth in Benchmark. Run the seeded comparison and export results.
